Positive variance means actuals were higher than the estimate. Review the source records before changing your pricing. Add a labor rate to compare hours and dollars on the same footing; add a job price too to see margin, not just cost.

Common questions

What counts as “other costs” in this calculator?

Other costs is any non-labor, non-materials line billed against the job — permits, equipment rental, disposal fees, a subcontractor invoice, or anything else that isn't wages or material purchases. The calculator treats it exactly like materials: it adds the estimated and actual figures into total cost and reports the difference as its own line, so a permit fee that ran over doesn't get buried inside a materials number.

Why is my cost variance shown with a minus sign?

A minus sign means materials and other costs together came in under estimate — actual spend was lower than what was quoted. No sign (shown as a plus) means actual costs ran higher than estimated. The sign is arithmetic, not a verdict: a large negative variance is still worth reviewing, since it can mean a bid was priced high rather than run efficiently.

Does this calculator store or upload my job numbers?

No. All six inputs are read from the form and the arithmetic runs in your browser; nothing is sent to a server, saved to an account, or logged anywhere. Closing the tab clears every figure you typed, so copy the review before you navigate away if you want to keep it.

Should I run this before or after the job is finished?

After. The tool compares an estimate against what actually happened, so it needs both sets of numbers — labor hours actually worked, materials actually bought, and other costs actually billed. Running it mid-job with partial actuals will still produce a variance, but it will be a snapshot of work in progress rather than the completed-job review the copyable report is written for.

vs-checking-if-you-still-made-money.html.text:
← Job Margin Variance

This calculator vs. just checking if you still made money

The fastest job review there is: does the final invoice clear the bid? It catches an outright loss and nothing else -- a job can still turn a profit while quietly losing more than a tenth of its margin, and the line actually responsible is rarely the one that looks biggest on the invoice.

What each check actually tells you

Checking whether you still made money is one comparison: total cost against the bid price, after the fact. It answers exactly one question -- loss or no loss -- and nothing about where the job moved or which assumption to fix before quoting the next one like it. It needs no tool at all, which is exactly why it is the default.

This calculator takes the same estimate-versus-actual numbers and breaks them into labor hours, materials, and other costs, each measured on its own line. Add an hourly rate and it prices the labor-hour variance in the same currency as the other two, so the three lines can be ranked against each other honestly instead of comparing a raw hours count to two dollar figures. Add the bid price as well and it turns that into the actual margin swing -- the number "we still made money" cannot see.

Estimate vs. actualEstimatedActualVariance
Labor hours (at $55/hr)16 hrs20 hrs+4 hrs -- $220
Materials$420$465$45
Other costs$80$95$15
Job price$2,000
Profit$620 (31.0%)$340 (17.0%)−$280, −14.0 points

"Did we still make money?" answers yes -- $340 profit, still positive. It stops there. This calculator's own defaults show the fuller picture: margin fell from 31.0% to 17.0%, a 14-point swing, and of the $280 total cost increase, $220 of it -- nearly 79% -- is the 4 extra labor hours priced at the $55/hr rate, not the $45 materials overrun that looks like the bigger number sitting next to a bare "4" on an unpriced hours line. Revise the next quote's materials allowance on the strength of the flat check and the estimate stays wrong in the same place.

QuestionWhere to answer it
Did the job clear the bid at all?Either check answers this -- a flat total-vs-bid comparison is enough for a yes/no.
By how many points did the margin actually move?This calculator's margin section, once a labor rate and bid price are entered.
Which single assumption is most worth revising before the next quote?This calculator's ranked largest-movement line -- priced in dollars, not a raw hours count next to two dollar figures.
Is a labor overrun hiding behind a smaller-looking materials number?This calculator, once an hourly rate is entered -- a flat total-vs-bid check cannot separate the two at all.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and nothing you type is uploaded.

Common questions

Isn't it enough to check whether the invoice cleared the bid?

It catches an outright loss and nothing else. On this calculator's own worked example -- 16 estimated hours running to 20, materials $420 to $465, other costs $80 to $95, a $55/hr rate and a $2,000 bid -- the job still nets $340 profit, down from an estimated $620. A flat before/after check sees a job that made money and stops there. It does not see that the margin fell from 31% to 17%, or which of the three lines actually did it.

Which line actually caused the overrun in that example?

Labor, by a wide margin, and it is the line a flat total hides best. Materials ran $45 over and other costs $15 over -- $60 combined, and the more visible number on an invoice. But 4 extra labor hours at $55/hr is a $220 overrun -- nearly 79% of the full $280 cost increase -- and it never appears as a dollar figure on the invoice at all unless someone prices the hours at the shop rate.

Why does a raw hours number get missed next to two dollar figures?

Because eyeballing a materials line, an other-costs line, and an hours line side by side means comparing $45 and $15 against a bare "4" -- different units read as if they were the same one. $45 looks bigger than 4 on the page, so materials gets blamed and the estimate gets revised on the wrong assumption. This calculator prices the hours at your rate before ranking, so the comparison is dollars against dollars, not dollars against a bare count.

Do I need to add a labor rate and bid price to use this?

No -- both are optional. Without them the calculator still reports the cost variance and flags the largest-moving line by its own unit. Adding an hourly rate converts the labor-hour variance into the same currency as materials and other costs, so the ranking is not comparing hours to dollars. Adding the job's bid price on top turns that into the margin swing -- the number that actually says whether "we still made money" is hiding a real problem.

vs-quickbooks-job-costing.html.text:
← Job Margin Variance

This calculator vs. QuickBooks Job Costing

Two different shapes: QuickBooks Online's job costing tracks every booked transaction against a project, inside a full ongoing accounting subscription. This page is a free, private six-field worksheet for one question — where did this one already-finished job move from estimate to actual, and what should that change about the next quote.

What each tool is for

QuickBooks Online Job Costing lives behind the Projects feature on the Plus and Advanced plans. Every invoice, bill, expense, and timesheet entry gets tagged to a project as the job runs, QuickBooks Time supplies the labor hours, and the Project Profitability report totals whatever was actually booked in the books over the job's life — estimates, transactions, and outstanding invoices in one dashboard. It is accurate exactly to the extent every transaction was tagged correctly, and it requires the accounting system underneath it: a chart of accounts, bank feeds or manual entry, and an ongoing subscription. QuickBooks' own pricing and plan details are not repeated here, since this session cannot verify today's exact figures against Intuit's current pricing page; only its well-documented feature set and plan structure are described.

This calculator does none of what QuickBooks' job costing does. It has no ledger, no chart of accounts, and no memory between visits. It takes six numbers you already have once a job is finished — estimated and actual labor hours, materials, and other costs, read off a spreadsheet, invoice, or job folder — and returns the cost variance, the labor-hour variance, whichever line moved the most (in matching units if you add a labor rate), and, if you add the job's bid price too, the estimated margin, actual margin, and the margin swing between them. It runs free in any browser, needs no account and no bookkeeping setup, and uploads nothing you type.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I run my whole business's books through QuickBooks and want every job's profitability tracked automatically as invoices and bills come in.QuickBooks Online Job Costing (Projects) — that ongoing, transaction-level tracking is what it is built for.
A job just finished and I have the estimated and actual hours and costs in a spreadsheet or job folder — where did the number move, and by how much?This calculator — free, instant, private, no account or bookkeeping setup.
I do not use QuickBooks, or my books are not tagged by project, but I still want one job's variance.This calculator — it needs only the six figures for that one job, nothing else in the accounting system.
I want the margin swing, not just the raw cost variance, once I add the bid price.This calculator's optional labor-rate and job-price fields turn cost variance into an estimated-vs-actual margin comparison.
I need the same profitability view across every open and closed job, tied to real booked transactions.QuickBooks Online Job Costing — built for the fleet view, not a single job's before/after comparison.
Do I need to create an account or tag transactions to use the tool?This calculator: no. QuickBooks Job Costing is used through an ongoing, tagged accounting subscription.

Most contractors get different value from each: QuickBooks (or a comparable accounting platform) for a running, transaction-accurate profitability record across every job, and a private calculator like this one for an instant, no-login read on where one already-finished job moved and which assumption to revisit before the next quote. This page's own figures are a completed-job review, not a ledger, an invoice record, or a substitute for bookkeeping.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or QuickBooks Job Costing?

They do different jobs. QuickBooks Online's job costing lives behind the Projects feature on the Plus and Advanced plans: every invoice, bill, expense, and timesheet entry gets tagged to a project as it happens, and the Project Profitability report totals whatever was actually booked over the job's life, integrated with QuickBooks Time for labor hours. It requires an ongoing accounting subscription, a chart of accounts, and consistent tagging discipline to be accurate. This calculator does none of that. It takes six numbers you already have after a job is done — estimated and actual labor hours, materials, and other costs — and returns the cost variance, labor-hour variance, the single largest movement, and optionally the margin swing, instantly, in the browser, with no account, no bookkeeping setup, and nothing uploaded. A contractor running their whole business's books through QuickBooks is better served finishing that setup; a contractor who wants a fast, private read on one already-finished job, without opening the accounting system, is in the right place here.

why-did-my-job-cost-more-than-i-estimate.text:
← Job margin variance calculator

Why did my job cost more than I estimated?

A finished job that cost more than the quote usually has one line that moved the most — a materials price that jumped, hours that ran long, or a small "other costs" line nobody watched. Finding that line by eye across three separate comparisons is slower than the arithmetic, and it is easy to fixate on the wrong one.

Open the free job margin variance calculator

What a single total variance cannot see

Labor hours and dollars are different units. A job can run 4 hours over on labor and $45 over on materials at the same time — knowing which of those two is the bigger problem for the next quote takes comparing them side by side, not just a total dollar figure.

The largest movement is not always the total. Total cost variance combines materials and other costs; the single largest line can be either one of those, and it's the line worth reviewing first, not the combined total.

A record fades fast. The reasons behind an overrun — a supplier price change, an access delay, extra prep — are easiest to remember and log right after the job, before the next quote repeats the same estimate.

A number you can defend

  1. Enter estimated and actual labor hours, materials cost, and other costs from the completed job.
  2. Read the variance on each of the three lines — actual minus estimate, in that line's own unit.
  3. Check the total cost variance (materials plus other costs) against the estimate.
  4. Note the single largest movement the calculator flags, and copy the review into the job folder before quoting similar work again.

Worked example

A job estimated at 16 labor hours, $420 in materials, and $80 in other costs actually ran 20 hours, $465 in materials, and $95 in other costs. Labor ran 4 hours over. Materials ran $45 over. Other costs ran $15 over. Total cost variance (materials plus other costs) is $60 above estimate. Comparing the three movements, materials is the largest single line to review — the $45 swing outweighs both the labor-hour overrun and the smaller other-costs line — so that's the assumption to revisit before quoting the next similar job.

Common questions

Why did my job cost more than I estimated?

Enter the estimated and actual figures for labor hours, materials, and other costs from the completed job. The calculator computes the variance on each line and reports total cost variance — actual materials and other costs minus estimated — in the same currency as the job, plus which single line moved the most.

Which number should I look at first after a job — labor hours or materials cost?

Whichever line has the largest movement, reviewed line by line: labor-hour variance, materials variance, and other-cost variance are each measured in their own unit, and the largest single movement is flagged as the assumption most worth reviewing before the next similar quote.

How do I use this to fix future quotes?

Run the comparison immediately after the job closes, while the reasons for any overrun are still fresh, then copy the review into the job folder. The next time you quote similar work, check the assumption this report flagged as the largest mover before you repeat the same estimate.
